about: The 17 data traps every NISAR user meets, in three groups, plus 'limits': things radar can never prove. Each card: what fools you, how we proved it, how OmniSAR handles it. inApp = whether that handling is already built into this version of the app.

traps.title: Raw NISAR files are huge, in a science format, behind a login
traps.fools: You expect to open a picture. Instead each file is hundreds of MB to several GB of HDF5, and downloading needs a NASA Earthdata login.
traps.proof: The official radar image files we use are about 5 GB each; interferogram files are 2–2.5 GB.
traps.handling: We download and process the files once, and the app ships only small results. Visitors never log in or download anything.

traps.title: NASA's NISAR map tiles break at close zoom
traps.fools: Zoom in past level 9 (about 280 m pixels) and the tile server sends random garbage or errors that look like real detail.
traps.proof: We asked NASA's server for the same zoom-10 NISAR tile 5 times on 14 Nov 2026 and got 4 different images back (on 13 Nov: 4 different images in 5 requests, from two networks).
traps.handling: OmniSAR never takes a number from NISAR map tiles: every value comes from the science files. Sharper views use other satellites, always labelled.

traps.title: Published date lists lag behind reality
traps.fools: The server's list of available dates stopped at 23 Oct, so you would think there was no newer data.
traps.proof: Tiles for 28–29 Oct existed and loaded even though the list didn't include them.
traps.handling: Pass dates come from NASA's file catalogue (CMR), which lists every real file, not from the tile server's date list.

traps.title: The colour meaning isn't written on the map
traps.fools: The NISAR map is in false colour, but the map server doesn't say what the colours mean.
traps.proof: It is in ASF's NISAR documentation: red and blue show HH (the direct echo), green shows HV (the plant-and-roughness echo).
traps.handling: Our measurements read HH and HV separately from the radar files, and every map has a legend.

traps.title: Most dates are blank
traps.fools: NISAR images strips of the Earth, so on most days there is simply no image of your place. A blank day is not a 'no change' day.
traps.proof: Scanning every date from Oct 2025 to Nov 2026 for four UAE points found images only every 12 days or so.
traps.handling: The timeline shows only the real pass dates for each case, taken from NASA's catalogue.

traps.title: No NISAR data over the UAE before 18 June 2026
traps.fools: With no radar images before June, it's tempting to treat the area as 'empty' or unchanged before then.
traps.proof: The same date scan, plus a check across a 1,000 km-wide area, found nothing before 18 Jun 2026.
traps.handling: We only make claims from 18 Jun onward. Anything earlier would need another satellite (Sentinel-1), clearly labelled.

traps.title: Passes come from two directions
traps.fools: NISAR passes over the same place going north (ascending) and going south (descending). They look at slopes and walls from opposite sides, so comparing one with the other shows 'change' that is only the viewing angle.
traps.proof: Over the UAE, passes arrive in pairs of days, one ascending and one descending, and slopes look different in each.
traps.handling: Each case compares passes from one direction only, and the case card says which track it uses.

traps.title: Interference makes fake glowing patches
traps.fools: Other radio signals on Earth leak into the radar and paint bright blobs. Compare two single dates and a blob looks like a huge change.
traps.proof: In our Jebel Ali box, HH on 28 Oct 2026 was 6.3 dB brighter than on 18 Jun, while the whole NISAR frame moved only 0.1 dB. A two-date comparison would call almost the whole box 'new'.
traps.handling: We compare every pass with the whole frame, use the median of several passes, and don't report a radar-only area while a pass is contaminated.

traps.title: Mountains create fake change
traps.fools: Steep slopes facing towards or away from the satellite change brightness with the viewing angle, which can look like change.
traps.proof: Jebel Hafeet showed 'change' that is a viewing-angle effect.
traps.handling: Changes on rugged ground are marked low confidence, using elevation data.

traps.title: Speckle: radar graininess
traps.fools: Single radar pixels jump up and down between dates even when nothing changed.
traps.proof: Single pixels jump up and down between dates in the NISAR images we compared.
traps.handling: We average each 3×3 block of 10 m pixels (30 m result) before comparing dates, and ignore changed patches smaller than about 1 hectare.

traps.title: Calm water and dry sand look the same
traps.fools: Both are smooth, so the radar beam bounces away and both come back dark. 'New water' in a desert may just be dry sand.
traps.proof: In our Jebel Ali box on 18 Jun 2026, open sea measured −17.1 dB in HH and desert sand −16.9 dB: practically the same.
traps.handling: Before reporting water turning into land (or back), OmniSAR checks whether sea and sand can be told apart on those dates. At Jebel Ali they can't, so we don't report it.

traps.title: Cities hide floods
traps.fools: Buildings bounce the radar strongly, so floodwater between them doesn't look dark the way open water does.
traps.proof: During the March 2026 storm, NASA's radar water map barely flagged flooded Dubai streets (first look).
traps.handling: Flood labels in cities are marked low confidence.

traps.title: Map tiles are pictures, not measurements
traps.fools: The NISAR map tiles are pre-coloured images. Their colours are not calibrated radar values, so you can't measure from them.
traps.proof: The tiles are 8-bit coloured PNG/JPEG images; the calibrated values are only in the science files.
traps.handling: Every number in a verdict comes from the calibrated science files, never from tile colours.

traps.title: Ground-motion files: huge, uncorrected, with a gap
traps.fools: Interferogram (InSAR) files are 2–2.5 GB each, the atmosphere corrections are included but not applied, and there is a NASA data gap from 27 Jul to 10 Aug 2026.
traps.proof: For Jakarta we used 16 NASA interferogram files (2.3 GB each) and read only a 17 × 33 km box from each. The ionosphere and troposphere corrections are stored as extra layers, not applied; NASA has no data from 27 Jul to 10 Aug 2026; and the descending frame we downloaded covers only part of our box.
traps.handling: We read only the box, apply the stored corrections ourselves, bridge the gap with 24-day pairs, and say when a direction can't be used.

traps.title: Humid air and changing surfaces fake or hide motion
traps.fools: Water vapour slows the radar signal, which looks like the ground moved. Surfaces that change between passes scramble the measurement.
traps.proof: In our Jakarta pairs, humid air alone shifts the signal by 6-31 mm across the box, and the ionosphere by 4-46 mm, in just 12 days. Water, fields and building sites drop below 0.4 coherence.
traps.handling: We subtract NASA's air corrections, mask coherence below 0.4, chain 8 pairs, and use two directions (dawn and dusk) when both are usable.

traps.title: Sea-level rise is too slow to see
traps.fools: Sea level rises a few millimetres a year. A few months of radar can't show it.
traps.proof: Global sea level rises by millimetres per year (citation pending). In each of our 12-day Jakarta pairs, the air alone moves the signal by up to 46 mm.
traps.handling: OmniSAR measures land motion, not sea level, and says so.

traps.title: Soil moisture data is coarse
traps.fools: NASA's SMAP soil moisture comes in 9 km squares, much bigger than one hillside.
traps.proof: The SMAP grid is 9 km; the slopes we study are a few hundred metres across.
traps.handling: Soil moisture is used only as regional wet or dry; slope comes from 30 m elevation data.

limits.title: Radar can't see who, why, legality or the future
limits.fools: A clear change makes it tempting to name who did it, say it broke a rule, or predict what will happen next.
limits.proof: Radar measures how the ground scatters microwaves: how bright it is and, with InSAR, how it moves. Nothing in the signal records who owns a place, whether something was allowed, why it was done, or what will happen.
limits.handling: OmniSAR only states what changed, where, when, and how sure we are. A cause appears only with a cited source. No accusations and no forecasts.
